newsitem.title: UK: BA braced as strike countdown begins.
newsitem.headline: BA braced as strike countdown begins.

text.p: British Airways Plc braced itself for its second strike ballot result in days on Monday as trade unions counted votes of BA ground staff in favour of striking and analysts warned the cost of confrontation would be heavy if passengers defected.
The Transport and General Workers Union (T&G) claimed this latest ballot, of 9,000 ground staff, would show overwhelming strike support, with the result due at 1400 GMT.
If BA ground staff give the go-ahead, it will be a double-blow for BA which saw cabin crew pass a 73 percent vote in favour of strike in a separate ballot last week.
The two ballots stem from different issues but are both linked to BA's cost-cutting moves to save 1.0 billion pounds ($1.7 billion) by 2000.
Cabin crew are protesting over a five-month-long row over a new pay structure pay row and ground staff are resisting the planned sale of BA's catering division.
If ground staff also vote yes to striking, BA could face disruption on ground and in the air simultaneously. Union bosses will meet this evening to discuss the ballot results and tactics.
BA's share price was under pressure ahead of the result, with the shares down nine pence at 686-1/2 by 1150 GMT.
Analysts said the impact on BA profits could be heavy, especially if passengers decided to start switching airlines.
"A strike would make a massive difference to BA -- financially in the short term as well as hurting it long-term," said Chris Avery, analyst at Paribas.
Avery warned that BA's lucrative business traveller community would not be likely to take on a strike risk.

"As a businessman, if there's a risk that you won't get to a meeting in Tokyo or New York in two weeks' time due to the threat of disruption, you will book with someone else now. Not wait until tomorrow."
"What you have to consider is people who switch away may find it's not so bad elsewhere and BA then faces the task of having to win customers back."
Industry observers pointed out that when BA faced the threat of a pilots' strike last year, which failed to materialise, the cost to profits was far from negligible.
"That dispute cost them more than 10 million pounds," said another transport analyst, even though no action took place.
The losses stemmed from worried customers switching to other airlines after months of dragged out rows with BA pilots. "It's just an indication of the cost of disruption this time round," said Avery.
British Airways has made it clear that it takes the threat seriously, unveiling strong-arm tactics in recent days to break the strike mood.
It told staff over the weekend strikers could be sacked and sued for damages.

BA has also drawn up a battle-plan to keep services flying. All management have been re-trained to allow them to take on more roles, extra security will be brought in to get strike breakers through picket-lines and the group is also willing to hire external staff to take on BA strikers' jobs.
"BA is staking a lot on this," said one travel industry insider. "It's investing a lot of money and ruling by fear. Not very nice. But I guess that's commerce."

The airline, fresh from a 60 million pounds facelift and in the midst of seeking regulatory clearance for its alliance with AMR's American Airlines, has placed all operations on red alert to combat the threat.
Chief Executive Robert Ayling cancelled his planned trip to witness the handover of Hong Kong in order to take on British unions instead.
"The big issue for BA is control of its cost base," summed up one transport analyst. "BA needs to win this one and end the showdown with the unions for good." ($ = 0.601 British Pounds)
